punched-cards: Holes punched in card or paper that a machine reads as instructions or data. Bouchon steered a loom with punched paper in 1725; Jacquard, Babbage and Hollerith built on it.
galvanometer: A coil of wire around a magnetized needle: current through the coil swings the needle. Schweigger's 1820 multiplier made weak currents measurable.
camera: A light-tight box with a lens that throws an image onto a screen, plate or film. Zahn's 1685 portable camera obscura was the box Niépce and Daguerre put their plates in.
keys: A hand-pressed lever or switch that turns a press of the finger into a signal or a stroke. Vail's 1837 telegraph key was one; a keyboard is a row of them.
electron-gun: A cathode and charged plates that shoot a narrow beam of electrons. Braun's 1897 tube had one; picture tubes, camera tubes and electron microscopes are built around it.
photocell: A cell that turns light into an electric current. Elster and Geitel made a practical one in 1893.
lithium-battery: A small, long-lasting battery with a lithium anode, first sold in the early 1970s.
mercury: A metal that is liquid at room temperature, known since antiquity. It went into barometers, thermometers, mirror backing and amalgam fillings.
escapement: Lets a clock's stored energy out in equal ticks. The verge escapement made weight-driven clocks possible in the late 1200s; the anchor escapement followed in 1657.
ink: Pigment or dye in a liquid that marks a surface. Egyptian and Chinese scribes made carbon ink by 2500 BCE; Gutenberg needed an oil-based one for his press.
gun-lock: The mechanism that sets off a gun's charge: the matchlock (about 1411), then the wheellock, flintlock and percussion cap.
sulfur: A yellow element known since antiquity as brimstone. It goes into gunpowder, sulfuric acid and vulcanized rubber.
gasoline: A light fraction of petroleum, at first a waste product of kerosene refining, that became the fuel for car engines and early rockets.
zinc: A metal smelted in India for centuries and isolated in Europe by Marggraf in 1746. Batteries use it up to make current.
lead: A soft, heavy metal worked since prehistory. It went into type metal, storage-battery plates and leaded gasoline.
quartz-oscillator: A sliver of quartz that vibrates at a steady frequency when driven by a current. Cady built one in 1921; quartz clocks followed in 1927.
